title.zh: 尼夫尼塔克：以膂力抗老

region.en: Northern hunting grounds and the foreign coast across the ice
region.zh: 北方獵場與冰海彼岸的異鄉

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Greyless among grown grandchildren, Nivnitak shames them back to the ice by hunting alone through the worst winter, following a sledge-track clean across the frozen sea to a foreign coast. Married there to two daughters of a faster hunter, he out-eats his host, out-hauls him, and — wearing a jacket of still-warm seal-entrails — wins the ball-play both ways, first knocked flat by his own wish 'I only wish I may do well,' then uncatchable. Slipping away in a glued-tight suit, he leaves a moss-stuffed decoy in a snow-hut for the pursuers to spear, and dies at last at home at a very old age, flesh shrivelled and shrunk.
summary.zh: 孫輩皆已成年而他猶無一根白髮的尼夫尼塔克，嚴冬獨自出獵，令賴床的子孫羞愧重返冰上。他循雪橇轍跡橫越冰海，抵達異鄉海岸；娶了比他更快的老獵手的兩個女兒——比食量、比拖曳、以尚帶體溫的豹腸新衣赴賽。擲球戲上他先是心願『但願我能打好』而被球擊倒，再戰則無人能敵。他縫製緊身衣夜遁，以塞苔草的假人誘敵刺殺，安然返鄉，直至壽終。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads the tale as enshrining the esteem for personal dexterity, strength, courage, and hardihood brought to bear against old age. Entrails-jacket detail documented as told.

passages.text: Nivnitak went away and settled far off to the north, at a certain place favourably situated for all kinds of hunting. He had many grandchildren, who all grew up to be skilled hunters while he was still in the prime of life; but none of them ever came to be a match for him. At last they also married in their turn and begat children before Nivnitak had got one grey hair. It once happened that the winter set in very severely, with hard weather every day; when the sea was getting all covered with ice the young people gradually left off hunting, while Nivnitak was constantly on the move, alternately on land and on the frozen sea. Later on the young men did not even rise from their couches. 'To-morrow I won't go out hunting, but I intend to climb the highest mountains to have a survey of the sea' — and returning late: 'I climbed the highest, and saw the frost-smoke at different places far out at sea. No doubt there will be animals to be got there; to-morrow I shall try.' When the midnight stars shone brightest he left the house, gained the outermost islets at dawn, and for the first time observed the haze hanging above the open water; pushing a seal on before him, he entered the house: 'If we are in want of game, I have found a hole where plenty of seals, large as well as small, are to be had.' His children and grandchildren only murmured and sulked a little, then asked for a morsel of blubber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Again off at an early hour, he returned late at night covered with sweat with a very large seal; that day the young men had risen and were sitting on the ledge with their boots on; the following night they were mending their hunting tools, and on the ensuing morning some of the ablest accompanied him — but because of their slowness he ordered them not to attack the larger seals. At the aperture he detected the marks of a sledge leading right out to sea, examined them closely, lanced a couple of seals, and dragging them along by the tug-line made for home — but finding his grandchildren, each with but one seal, too slow for him, prepared to leave them: 'Ye know your way, of course, and can go on by yourselves,' reaching home much earlier. 'If the weather stands, it is quite a treat to go out hunting; now ye may stop at home if ye like: I will take care that we do not suffer from want of food.' On the morrow he left as usual, but in the evening they expected him back in vain: Nivnitak remembered the track of the sledge, and having found it, followed it across the sea; the mountains of his own country were lost to sight, others appeared ahead, and he landed on a foreign coast at the opposite side of the ocean.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Passing through a valley he beheld a sheet of frozen water, and close by a little house with some poles stuck in the ground beside it; a woman emerged, and perceiving a stranger approaching by such an unwonted road, stood hesitating an instant, then asked him to come inside — two young girls sitting close to the wall, whom he secretly determined should be his future wives. He felt very hungry and hoped to be offered something to eat, but was disappointed; one of the women returned crying 'Yonder he is coming!' — through the window Nivnitak saw a man running along the ice at a great rate, tugging two seals after him, disappearing among the loose ice-blocks near the beach, then reappearing bounding towards the house — stopping at seeing the outer garments of a stranger hung on the poles. Having relieved himself of his clothes, the host took a bear-skin from beneath the ledge, spreading it mid-way on the floor: 'When two men meet for the first time they always try to outdo each other; let us have a try.' Nivnitak did not hesitate a moment, undressed, sat down opposite, hooked his hand into his adversary's arms, and pulled away with all might, almost succeeding in mastering him. The host seated himself on the main ledge and inquired if the visitor had got anything to eat — 'No' — 'Why, then, make haste and treat him to your best' — the women set forth several dishes, and when the host was going to begin the dish was already empty. He looked at the two girls flensing the seal on the floor, one cleaning the entrails, the other blowing them up; before the seal-flesh was boiled the entrails had been dried, and the girls were busy making a jacket of them for their father.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I am in want of a companion on my hunting excursions; we have plenty of good hunting hereabout. Away on the ice is a place where the thong-seals have their breathing-holes... If thou wantest a wife, thou art welcome to take one of my daughters' — and thus Nivnitak became his son-in-law. Next day the father put on the jacket of seal-entrails from yesterday's hunt; they wandered a great distance on the ice till they reached the apertures made by the seals — 'As thou hast not got my alacrity thou hadst better not catch more than one at a time; it is as much as I can manage to drag along two of them.' Meanwhile he soon caught a couple; Nivnitak thought he should like to do the same, and when he had caught the first and the father-in-law had turned a little aside, hastened to pull up another, and thus had two. Hauling their seals along, the host continually observed the sun, guiding himself by it — 'I suppose thou knowest thy way by this time; I think I will leave thee to follow in my wake.' 'We cannot expect him before late, but still ye must keep a look-out for him,' said the father on entering the main room; the daughters kept waiting and waiting, but he did not come home till late in the night. The father-in-law never spoke to him, but the daughters were delighted to see him and at once cut up the animals — but when they were preparing to make the dress, the entrails had shrunk and got too small: this was the reason the father made such haste in returning, that the entrails might not get cold on the way, lest they should shrink and be unfit for use. He was now displeased at having got a son-in-law not as clever as he wished him to be.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They went out together all the same next day with a similar result; on the way home the father again told him that as he could not keep up with him he would go on beforehand — but this time Nivnitak was saying to himself, 'To-day I should just like to run a race with him.' He soon lost sight of him and lost his way besides, but at the same time felt that his burden was getting lighter; continuing to run still faster, turning round he saw that his two seals were swinging round in the air after him. He passed by his host in a great circuit and was home in good time long before him; his wife instantly prepared the meal, and seeing the blown-up entrails clean and shining, Nivnitak did not doubt they would make him a nice jacket. He let the meat be kept ready dressed for his father-in-law, and the women had the jacket finished even before his arrival; putting it on at once he was standing outside mending his tools when the host made his appearance — at first sight he thought some visitor had arrived during his absence, and not till he had passed the iceberg did he recognise Nivnitak; on finding it to be him he was very well pleased, and again spoke familiarly: 'That's right, we will always succeed in the end' — but Nivnitak did not quite understand this speech. Seated at the meal, the host said, 'Why, it has been getting quite cold and dry' — he did not quite like it so; nevertheless he was as gay and talkative as could be. They now went on having the same good luck, and Nivnitak totally forgot his home and his grandchildren, and would not leave his young wives.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day his father-in-law accosted him: 'The moon is now in the crescent, and our neighbours will be coming to pay us a visit and practice ball-playing; to-morrow I shall stay at home and make tools for the games, and we must all be smart and trim in new dresses.' Next day Nivnitak likewise stayed at home, and his father-in-law brought in six large shoulder-blades of walrus: 'When the play has begun, and the ball has been thrown, we must follow its course, and always be ready to strike it; if any one throws it wrong we shan't win; so thou must mind what thou art about. With this spoon-like instrument we hit the ball; I shall throw it to my wife, and she to her daughter, and they will send it on to thee; take care that thou dost not make any mistake, or miss catching it, lest we should be mocked and scorned.' At last a great many people appeared passing round the southern point, and Nivnitak, along with his new relations, quickly put on his new clothes and ran out to meet them on the ice, shouting to them, 'Here we are with our new relative Nivnitak! Let the play begin at once!' — the strangers answered with a loud yell. The ball, consisting of a large seal-skin stuffed with sand and clay, and fashioned like a real seal, was now brought out; the master determined that Nivnitak, being the most dexterous, should stand next to the adversaries, and began the play by throwing the ball to his wife; she running along beneath it thrust it to her younger daughter, she in her turn to her elder sister, and she to her husband — but when Nivnitak was about to strike it, he thought to himself, 'I only wish I may do well.' That instant the ball hit him with its whole force and knocked him down, so that he was unable to rise; the enemies shouted and yelled in great triumph and took up the ball, carrying it towards their dwelling-place, their opponents pursuing without any result. On turning round the host saw a multitude of people and not observing Nivnitak among them suspected some evil; hurrying to his assistance he found him almost dying, some filling his clothes with snow, others actually trampling on him. He drew him from out the heap, but the enemies left with great glee and loud halloos; Nivnitak's clothes had been quite spoiled with the snow and the mud, and in this state they got home — the father-in-law sullen and cross.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'It will soon be time for us to pay our neighbours a return visit; get everything ready' — on departing Nivnitak looked very nice in his new suit, but the father-in-law once more admonished him: 'We must do our utmost to vanquish them, and if thou doest wrong this time, we will have nothing more to do with thee' — Nivnitak did not deign to answer. Approaching the abode of the neighbours, a tumultuous roar was raised to welcome them, the ball brought down on the ice, and they posted themselves as before. When it was Nivnitak's turn to strike, he gave the ball such a blow that it turned round in the air and then flew straight forward; the father-in-law's turn to run for it, but Nivnitak had already reached it and hit it a second time; the adversaries advanced to give it a stroke, but Nivnitak always forestalled them, sending it higher and higher aloft — nobody could cope with him, and thus he went on pursuing the ball until he at length reached home. Their rivals had at last to give in and retired very much dejected, and Nivnitak's host cried out to them, 'To-day ye lost the game, better luck next time!' On the way home he kept constantly repeating, 'That's right, we will always succeed in the end' — it was only now that Nivnitak understood what the other had meant by saying so before. Some time after, Nivnitak began to think of his old relatives whom he had left in poverty and want; one day returning from his hunt he said to his wives, 'Make me a suit of tight clothes, jacket, breeches, and boots' — they fitted him as if they had been glued on to his body, and where they were a little too wide he at once had them altered; he made the suit into a bundle and went to hide it beneath the boat, and from this time secretly planned to return to his own country.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One night, when the others were sound asleep, he tried to leap down on the floor; but on touching the edge of the bench one of his wives awoke, and he again went back and quietly lay down beside them — for several nights he repeated his attempts, always obliged to turn in again. One night he succeeded in getting down without anybody awaking; to make quite sure they were all fast asleep he again stepped up on the ledge, and finding the noise had awakened nobody, jumped down on the floor above the entrance of the room and gliding out noiselessly dressed himself in his tight clothes, then in his outer coat hanging on the poles outside. Taking hold of his spear he climbed the low roof of the house and sallied forth in the opposite direction he wanted to take, making circular tracks in the snow; after a while he jumped and crossed the little promontory, got down on the ice which stretched away as far as his own country, again making large round tracks, always leaping from one side to the other so that his family should not be able to be guided by his footmarks. Reaching a coast with a steep ascent covered with heath, he once more formed plenty of round circles on the ice, jumped ashore, climbed an edge of the rock, stuffed his outer coat well with moss, and again leaped down; on the ice he built a snow-hut and placed the stuffed coat inside it, spear in hand, with the back turned outwards, that it might resemble a living man. After this he again went back and climbed the steep rock, awaiting the arrival of the pursuers. At sunrise several people who had come out in search of him were to be seen on the ice, sometimes single, sometimes making joint efforts to find the track; at last, halting at the snow-house, they approached it cautiously — no sooner had the foremost detected the figure in the doorway than he thrust his spear straight at it, and Nivnitak heard them call out, 'Well, well, we ought to have kept a better watch upon him while he was with us, showing well enough that he was not a real man; but anyhow we have done with him now' — and they returned, satisfied that they had killed him. When they had quite disappeared, Nivnitak again leapt down the rocks. The sun was then high in the heavens; but before it had quite set he reached the shore of his own country and found his grandchildren, who had totally given him up, prospering and doing well. In the spring-time, when the ice had vanished, he got a fancy to go and see his native place; but having arrived there he determined to spend the rest of his days in this place, and did not travel any more. He lived to see his grandchildren's grandchildren, but at length the flesh of his body became all shrivelled and shrunk; and finally, at a very old age, he died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 36 'Nivnitak'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Brother Who Went to Akilinek: Invention of the Dog-Sledge
title.zh: 遠赴阿基利內克的兄長：狗橇的發明

region.en: Frozen sea crossing and Akilinek, the country beyond
region.zh: 冰海橫渡與彼岸的阿基利內克

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; nearly literally translated from one manuscript, widely known in Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: His sister vanished from the islets, leaving only a sledge-track leading seaward, the matchless hunter brings home — one by one, to his little sister's horror — a bear, an amarok, and an agshik to draw the sledge his father makes of hard knotted wood; rounding the coast at a day's drive that would take a boat from spring to autumn. Trusting the unbroken ice, he drives straight across the sea to Akilinek, finds his sister married with a baby, matches teams with her reindeer-driving husband, and carries home the children's clothes as a promise — fulfilled when the sledges come, the merry little sister leaps the boat-stands and frightens the visitors off, and the furious agshik, loosed in punishment, returns bloody-muzzled, having probably devoured them all.
summary.zh: 妹妹在外島失蹤，冰上只餘一道指向海中的雪橇轍跡。無敵的獵手先後領回——令幼妹驚呼的——一頭熊、一頭狼靈、一隻阿格希克怪獸，拉動父親特製的硬木雪橇；沿岸疾馳，一日之程抵舟行春至秋之遙。他賭冰未裂，直駛海心抵達阿基利內克，尋得已為人母的妹妹；與其馴鹿橇夫比試獸力，又攜外甥的衣物作為歸約。雪橇如約而至，活潑的小妹歡躍過船架，卻嚇得客人掉頭而逃；盛怒的阿格希克被放去追擊，歸來時嘴邊血污——多半把他們全數吞了。

sensitivity.note: Rink reads the tale as probably resting on a historical basis: the invention of dog-sledging or the teaming and training of some wild animal from which the Eskimo dog descended. Rink's note records a kukissook variant in which the cousin-version ends with the Akilinek brother-in-law torn to pieces and the child killed. The devouring ending recorded as told.

passages.text: An old man had a son and two daughters; his son being a first-rate hunter and provider, the father at length gave up kayaking himself. His son could overtake and outrun every animal on shore, and at sea was an excellent hand at harpooning; his eldest sister used to follow him along the shore, amusing herself by catching partridges in little traps, and generally got a good many. At a time when the sea was frozen over, they one day went away to the outermost islets; there the brother saw a fox and set off to pursue it. After a short absence among the islets he returned with the fox — but meanwhile the sister was gone. He looked for her everywhere and called out, but she did not come; at length he detected the trace of a sledge, but as it was growing dark, he had to go home without his sister. On his return he grew silent and reserved, but after a while said to his father, 'Oh how much I should like to have a sledge!' The father favoured the idea and at once set about making him one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Next morning the son set out on foot, returned at nightfall without having killed anything, and went to sleep without a word. In the morning he asked his father to provide him with some cords, saying he wanted to fetch home an animal to pull his sledge for him, and went off. Towards evening a strange noise was heard, and the little sister went outside to see what it was, but instantly returned in great alarm, exclaiming, 'Oh, what dreadful monster is this my dear brother has brought home with him?' When he entered, the father asked him what beast it was — 'Why, it is only a little bear I have caught to drag my sledge; I hope thou wilt make a harness for it; I want him to be trained shortly.' The father complied, and the son left off hunting for a while in order to train the bear. Another time he again returned late in the evening quite exhausted; the following morning he asked his father for still stronger cords, went away, and in the evening a strange noise was again heard, the little sister returning quite horrified, saying it was still more frightful than the last time — 'Oh, it's nothing but a little amarok I have caught to match the bear.' These two, however, could not agree, and he had often to use his whip to part them when they were going to fight; after training they pulled very well together. He wanted a third one, and having set out for it in the morning did not return till late at night, when his parents had long been quite miserable on account of his long absence; the next morning he applied for strings and lashings, but this time none but the very strongest would serve him. In the evening there was a terrible noise outside, for now he had got the bear, the amarok, and an agshik fighting each other; at length he had them all tamed and trained.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.

passages.text: His father, quite willing, made him a sledge of very hard wood with many knots in it; when the sea was frozen over he went out to try his team, following the coast southwards, and returned towards evening the same day. Questioned as to how far he had been, he answered: 'If thou wert to leave with a boat early in spring, thou wouldst not have reached the place I got at to-day before autumn. In going home we made great speed, but the bear got tired, and I was obliged to take him into the sledge beside me; but the agshik is incapable of tiring, and will be of great use to me.' The next day he travelled on in the same manner to the north, returning home at night, adding, 'The agshik, I find, is soon provoked, and goes off in a fury; he will be rather dangerous for strangers to encounter.' The ice now covering the sea all over, not having broken up although it had been very stormy, he supposed he might trust himself out on it; and the weather again became settled and beautiful. 'Don't ye remember the day I wandered out on the ice with my sister and lost her there? Since that day I have sought her far and near all over our country: where can she have gone to? Not even the bones of her corpse did I find; but on the day I lost her, in looking for her, I noticed the marks of a sledge on the ice, leading right to sea. Any other trace of her I have never seen; and therefore I should now like to go across to Akilinek, as I shall certainly not be at rest until I have found her.' The parents tried to persuade him to stay — 'It does not matter for thy sister, who has been lost to us for such a great length of time; don't go away in search of her as far away as that, but bear in mind thou art now our only provider. Out yonder is a cleft in the ice so wide that thou mayst never cross it' — 'To be sure my animals cannot swim; the bear only in some degree is capable of that: but if I don't succeed, I shall, of course, return.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the exact spot where he had formerly seen the trace of a sledge he turned right seawards, and after a while lost sight of the land; the bear got tired as before, and being only a hindrance, he took it on the sledge. Driving continually straight on, he again came in sight of land and observed the tracks of many sledges, seeing them in all directions on approaching the shore. Making fast his animals to an iceberg near the strand, he went to shore himself, and had not walked long before he saw a number of houses; after a while he advanced, found an entrance, walked up to a large house and went inside — and at once recognised his sister sitting down with a baby on her lap. Seating himself on the side bench, she also recognised him, and they began to speak to each other: 'On the same day thou left me to pursue thy fox, a man in a sledge happened to pass by; and in no time I was taken up and carried away to this place, and that is the reason why thou seest me here. I am married, but at present my husband is out as usual. However, I expect him home very soon, and when he comes thou must look at him well.' 'Since that day I have done nothing but try to find thee out; all over the country I have travelled in search of thee; how lucky it is that I find thee at last!' Whilst they sat waiting some one called out, 'There he is coming!' — looking out at the window the brother saw his sister's husband driving on towards the house with a number of young reindeer pulling his sledge; though he sped on at a good rate, the other thought his own animals still swifter, and considering himself quite a match for the new-comer, again seated himself without any further remark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the husband entered he kept his eyes constantly fixed on the visitor sitting beside his wife, and without a word to any one leaned back on the ledge, so that nothing but his heels resting on the edge of it were visible. The relatives being thus interrupted left off speaking for a time; however, she told her brother it was for fear of her husband, who used to speak very little, being of a shy disposition; on hearing this he came a little closer to them, and they began to converse together. The guest spoke of his happiness in seeing his sister so well off, and said that seeing she had such a good provider he would not trouble himself any more about her in future, further proposing that they should come and visit him and his parents on the opposite shore — but his brother-in-law did not fancy this much, giving as a pretext that the cold would be too severe for the children. Both now wanted to persuade him to stay, but he said he must needs go and look after his animals, without mention of what kind they were; his relatives gave him some of the children's clothes for a gift to the parents — he put them on his shoulders, went to his sledge, and departed. When he had got so far that he had lost sight of the land the bear again got tired, and was taken in beside him; on his return his parents rejoiced greatly at seeing the clothes of their daughter's little children, and on hearing that their long-missed daughter was coming to visit them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day during fine weather, when they were anxiously expecting them, sledges were seen coming across the ice, which made them all very happy, the little sister, of a merry temper, hardly able to contain her joy. When her sister's sledge had come still closer she gave a jump and bounded over the boat, which was put up on the boat-pillars — but all of a sudden the sledgers were seen to put about, probably taking fright at seeing her brother's animals and at the girl indulging in such wild pranks. They now called out loudly for them, and the parents were very much distressed and wept together. This sight made the son take pity on the old people, and to punish the fugitives he let loose the agshik, being the most furious of the lot, to pursue them. In a moment the sledgers as well as the agshik disappeared; but on his return the agshik was all bloody around the muzzle. In all likelihood he devoured them all; the brother did not go in search of them, as he did not expect any of them to be alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 37 'The Brother who went to Akilinek in search of his Sister'; not verbatim.
